title: Inference vs outside knowledge and overreach
blurb: Separate what a passage supports from what a reader assumes, and reject options that are true in real life but not in the text.
question: A passage says a town added a bike lane and lowered the speed limit on the same street, and cycling there then doubled. One answer says the bike lane caused the increase; another says protected bike lanes reduce crashes. Both sound reasonable. Why are both wrong as inferences from this passage?

teach.body: Formally, an inference is a conclusion supported by evidence in the text plus reasoning. An assumption is an unsupported belief the reader brings to the text. A prediction is a claim about what will happen next. In plain English: an inference stays inside the fence of the passage; an assumption climbs over it, often without the reader noticing. The HESI A2 rewards the first and sets traps with the second.

teach.h: Three kinds of 'reading between the lines'

teach.body:
Last spring, the city added a protected bike lane on Elm Street. During the same month, it lowered Elm Street's speed limit from 35 to 25 miles per hour. Since then, the number of cyclists counted on Elm Street on weekday mornings has doubled.

Supported inference: changes to Elm Street were followed by more cycling there. Assumption: the bike lane alone caused the increase (two changes happened at once). Outside knowledge: protected lanes reduce crashes (maybe true, but not in this text).

items: For each option, point to the sentence or sentences that support it. No line, no answer.
Ask whether the option needs any fact the passage does not give. If so, it is an assumption.
Check for overstatement: all, always, never, proves, only, every.
Check cause and effect: is it reversed, or does it pick one cause when the text gives several?
Keep the option that the text supports fully and that goes no further.

teach.h: Is it an inference or an assumption?

head: Overstated (needs huge support)
Qualified (easier to support)
rows: was followed by, was linked to
teach.caption: Qualified wording is not automatically correct, but extreme wording is wrong unless the text is just as extreme.

teach.h: True in life is not the same as supported here
teach.body: The answer must be supported by the text alone. Outside knowledge can neither make an option right nor rescue a wrong one. If a passage describes a cavity survey and an option says 'fluoride strengthens enamel', that may be true in a science class, but if the passage never says it, it is not an inference from the passage. Ask 'Does the passage say or imply this?', not 'Is this true?'

teach.caption: An option in the left circle only is a trap, however true it is.

teach.text: Two events in sequence are not proof of cause: B followed A does not mean A caused B. Watch also for reversed cause and effect (do happy people use the trail, or does the trail make people happy?) and for options that pick one cause when the passage names two changes made at the same time.

teach.body: Daniel Kim, applying to a respiratory therapy program, reads the Elm Street passage and is drawn to 'The bike lane doubled the number of cyclists.' He runs the test: which line says the lane caused it? None. The passage names two changes in the same month, so crediting the lane alone is an assumption. He chooses 'More people cycled on Elm Street after the street was changed', which every line supports.

items: Inference: supported by the text plus reasoning. Assumption: brought in by the reader.
Use the 'show me the line' test on every option.
Extreme words (all, always, never, proves) need equally extreme support.
True in real life does not mean supported by the passage.
Sequence is not cause; watch for reversed cause and effect and for multiple causes.

summary: You can now keep inferences inside the text, using the 'show me the line' test. You can also reject assumptions, outside-knowledge options, overstatements and faulty cause-and-effect conclusions, even when they sound true.

A.q:
Read the passage.

Grace volunteers at the animal shelter every Saturday morning. She arrives before the doors open, walks the dogs that have been there longest, and often stays after her shift to clean the kennels.

Which statement is an assumption rather than an inference supported by the passage?
options: Grace is committed to her volunteer work at the shelter.
Grace plans to study to become a veterinarian one day.
Grace gives extra attention to the dogs waiting longest.
Grace often gives more time than her shift requires.
A.why: Nothing in the passage mentions Grace's career plans. A reader who thinks 'animal lover, so future vet' is bringing in an assumption.

whyNot.0: Supported: arriving early and staying late to clean show commitment.
whyNot.2: Supported: she walks the dogs that have been there longest.
whyNot.3: Supported: she often stays after her shift to clean kennels.

A.q:
Read the passage.

In a small study at Lakeview College, students who took a 20-minute walk before an exam scored slightly higher, on average, than students who sat quietly for the same time. The researchers note that the study included 60 students, all from one introductory biology course.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
options: This study linked a short walk to slightly higher scores.
Walking before an exam will raise any student's test score.
Exercise increases blood flow to the brain and aids memory.
The students who walked had studied harder than the others.
A.why: The passage reports one small study with a slight average difference. The supported conclusion stays at that size: in this study, walking was linked to slightly higher scores.

whyNot.1: Overstatement: one study of 60 students cannot support a claim about any student.
whyNot.2: Outside knowledge: the passage never mentions blood flow or memory.
whyNot.3: Unsupported: the passage says nothing about how much either group studied.

A.q:
Read the passage.

Most of the clinic's patients who used the new online portal last year said it was easier than calling the front desk. A few older patients said they preferred to speak with a receptionist.

Which statement can be inferred from the passage?
options: The clinic offers patients more than one way to reach it.
Older patients dislike using the clinic's online portal.
The clinic will soon stop answering patients' phone calls.
The portal is easier to use than other clinics' portals.
A.why: Patients can use the portal, call the front desk or speak with a receptionist, so the passage supports that the clinic offers more than one way to reach it, though it never says so directly.

whyNot.1: Overgeneralization: a few older patients preferred a receptionist; that says nothing about older patients as a group.
whyNot.2: This is an unsupported prediction; nothing suggests the phones will stop.
whyNot.3: No other clinic's portal is mentioned, so no comparison is supported.

B.q:
Read the passage.

Last fall, Maple Street Elementary replaced the sugary drinks in its vending machines with water and milk. That same fall, the school added a second daily recess. By spring, the school nurse reported fewer students coming to her office with stomachaches.

Which statement is an unsupported assumption?
options: The school made more than one change during the same fall.
Students could no longer buy sugary drinks from the machines.
The nurse saw fewer stomachache visits by spring than before.
The vending machine change caused the drop in stomachaches.
B.why: Two changes happened at the same time, and the passage never says which, if either, caused the drop. Crediting the vending machines is an assumption.

whyNot.0: Supported: the drinks and the second recess both changed that fall.
whyNot.1: Supported: the sugary drinks were replaced with water and milk.
whyNot.2: Supported: the nurse reported fewer stomachache visits by spring.

B.q:
Read the passage.

A survey in the town of Ridgeway found that residents who use the new walking trail at least twice a week report better moods, on average, than residents who do not use it.

A reader concludes, 'Walking on the trail puts people in better moods.' Why is this conclusion not fully supported?
options: The survey compared trail users with residents who skip it.
Happier residents may be the ones who choose the trail.
The trail opened too recently to affect anyone's mood.
The survey asked about moods but not about trail use.
B.why: The survey shows a link, not a cause. The reverse could explain it: people who already feel good may be the ones who go walking. The reader's conclusion assumes one direction.

whyNot.0: Comparing users with non-users is how the survey found the link; a comparison group is a strength, not the gap in the reader's reasoning.
whyNot.2: The passage gives no opening date, so this is not a reason drawn from the text.
whyNot.3: Contradicts the passage: the survey grouped residents by how often they use the trail.

B.q:
Read the passage.

Ana has failed the parallel-parking part of her driving test once. Every evening this week she has practiced between two trash cans in her driveway, and yesterday she parked cleanly five times in a row. Her test is next Friday.

Which statement is a prediction rather than an inference about the present?
options: Ana is putting steady effort into her parking skills.
Parallel parking was a weak spot for Ana in the past.
Ana's parking has improved since she began practicing.
Ana will pass the parking part of her test on Friday.
B.why: This makes a claim about a future event. The other options draw conclusions about Ana's past or present from the clues.

whyNot.0: This is an inference about the present, supported by her nightly practice.
whyNot.1: This is an inference about the past, supported by her failed attempt.
whyNot.2: This is an inference about the present, supported by five clean parks in a row.

C.q:
Read the passage.

Every volunteer at Saturday's blood drive had to complete a one-hour safety training first. Jordan volunteered at the blood drive on Saturday. Several of the blood drive volunteers also helped at the food bank on Sunday.

Which statement must be true based on the passage?
options: Jordan completed the safety training.
Jordan helped out at the food bank on Sunday.
Every food bank helper trained for the drive.
Jordan led the safety training on Saturday.
C.why: Every blood drive volunteer had to complete the training, and Jordan was a blood drive volunteer, so Jordan must have completed it.

whyNot.1: Possible but not required: only 'several' volunteers helped on Sunday, and Jordan may not be one of them.
whyNot.2: Unsupported: food bank helpers who were not blood drive volunteers are never mentioned.
whyNot.3: Nothing says who led the training.

C.q:
Read the passage.

The town of Westfield began adding fluoride to its water supply in 2015. A 2024 survey of local dentists reported fewer cavities among children than a similar survey in 2014. The 2024 survey did not track whether children's brushing habits or diets had changed during those years.

Which statement is best supported by the passage?
options: Adding fluoride to Westfield's water caused the drop in cavities.
Fluoride strengthens the enamel that protects children's teeth.
Fewer cavities were reported, but other causes are not ruled out.
Westfield's children brushed their teeth more often by 2024.
C.why: The surveys show fewer cavities, and the passage itself notes that brushing and diet were not tracked. The supported statement reports the drop without claiming a cause.

whyNot.0: Assumption: the passage points out that other changes were not ruled out.
whyNot.1: Outside knowledge: this may be taught in science, but the passage never says it.
whyNot.3: Unsupported: the passage says brushing habits were not tracked.

C.q:
Read the passage.

When Dr. Patel asked whether anyone had questions, the lecture hall went quiet. Several students looked down at their notebooks, and one glanced at the clock. Dr. Patel smiled, closed her laptop and said, 'Then I'll see you all on Thursday. Bring your questions about the lab.'

Which inference is most strongly supported?
options: The students were confused by the material Dr. Patel had covered.
Dr. Patel was annoyed that none of the students had spoken up.
Thursday's lab will count toward the students' final grades.
Dr. Patel ended the class when no student asked a question.
C.why: She asks for questions, gets silence, closes her laptop and says she will see them Thursday: together these clues show she ended the class when no one asked anything.

whyNot.0: Assumption: silence could mean many things, and nothing points to confusion in particular.
whyNot.1: Contradicted: she smiled, which does not fit annoyance.

reteach.title: Think like a juror
reteach.question: A juror may decide a case only on the evidence shown in court, not on news stories or hunches. How does that rule match a HESI A2 inference question?

blocks.body: A juror who thinks 'people like him usually do it' is using an assumption. A juror who read about the case online is using outside knowledge. Both are told to set those aside and decide from the exhibits and testimony alone. On the HESI A2, the passage is the evidence. If an answer needs anything the passage did not 'show the court', it is out, however believable it is.

blocks.text: A juror cannot convict because two things happened one after the other. Neither can you: sequence alone does not prove cause.

explain.body: An inference can be traced to lines in the text. An assumption cannot: it comes from the reader's expectations or beliefs.

test.q:
Read the passage.

Mr. Bowen's garden produced so many tomatoes this summer that he left a basket of them on the sidewalk with a sign reading 'Free: help yourself.'

Which statement is an assumption, not an inference?
options: Mr. Bowen grew more tomatoes than he could use himself.
Mr. Bowen was willing to give some of his tomatoes away.
Mr. Bowen's garden had a productive tomato harvest.
Mr. Bowen does not like to eat tomatoes himself.
test.why: Nothing in the passage tells us his taste in food. Giving away extras is explained by having too many, not by disliking them.

whyNot.0: Supported: he had so many that he left a basket out for others.
whyNot.1: Supported: the sign says 'Free: help yourself.'
whyNot.2: Supported: the garden produced 'so many tomatoes'.

explain.body: An option can be true in the real world and still be wrong, because the passage does not say or imply it. Judge every option by the text alone.

test.q:
Read the passage.

The county health department will offer free hearing screenings at the public library on the first Tuesday of each month. Walk-ins are welcome, and each screening takes about ten minutes.

Which statement is supported by the passage?
options: Hearing loss often develops slowly as people get older.
A screening can be done without making an appointment.
Loud music is a leading cause of hearing loss in teens.
Hearing screenings are covered by most insurance plans.
test.why: 'Walk-ins are welcome' supports that no appointment is needed.

whyNot.0: Outside knowledge: the passage says nothing about how hearing loss develops.
whyNot.2: Outside knowledge: causes of hearing loss are never discussed.
whyNot.3: Outside knowledge: insurance is never mentioned, and the screenings are free.

explain.body: Words like all, always, never, every and proves claim more than most passages can support. Match the strength of the option to the strength of the evidence.

test.q:
Read the passage.

In a survey of 200 nursing students at one college, 140 said they study better in the morning than at night.

Which statement is best supported?
options: Nursing students study better in the morning than at night.
Most students surveyed said mornings suit their studying.
Studying at night lowers the grades of nursing students.
Every student at the college prefers to study in the morning.
test.why: 140 of 200 is 70 percent of those surveyed, so 'most students surveyed' matches the evidence exactly.

whyNot.0: Overgeneralization: it extends one college's survey to nursing students in general.
whyNot.2: Grades are never mentioned, and the survey reports preferences, not results.
whyNot.3: Overstatement: 60 of the 200 did not say they prefer mornings.

explain.body: If B followed A, A did not necessarily cause B. Check for other changes at the same time, and check whether the cause and effect could run the other way.

test.q:
Read the passage.

After the hospital cafeteria began posting calorie counts on its menu board in January, sales of salads rose. In the same month, the cafeteria cut the price of salads by a dollar.

Which statement is best supported?
options: Posting calorie counts caused salad sales to rise in January.
Lower prices are the main reason people choose a salad.
Salad sales rose after two changes made in the same month.
Customers stopped buying other foods once calories were posted.
test.why: Two changes happened in January, and the passage does not say which one raised sales. The supported statement reports the rise without naming a cause.

whyNot.0: Assumption: the price cut happened at the same time, so the cause is unclear.
whyNot.1: Assumption: it credits the price cut with no more support than the calorie counts have.
whyNot.3: Unsupported and extreme: sales of other foods are never mentioned.
